title: Differential
body:
The infinitesimal piece, $dx$, that an integral sums up and a derivative divides by. Worth one note
because this course uses more kinds of it than any other, and the element is usually the hard part
of setting up an integral.

$$
dy = f'(x)\,dx
$$

Read as: a small change in $x$ produces a change in $y$ of about $f'(x)$ times as much. That is
[[Linear Approximation]] written multiplicatively, and it is where the [[Derivative]] gets its
$\frac{dy}{dx}$ notation. In several variables the same statement is the **total differential**

$$
df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy
$$

which is the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] with the $dt$s cancelled out of it.

## The elements used in this course

| Element | Is | Appears in |
|---|---|---|
| $dx$ | length along an axis | ordinary integrals |
| $ds$ | arc length along a curve | [[Line Integral]], [[Arc Length]] |
| $d\mathbf{r}$ | vector displacement along a curve | work, circulation |
| $dA$, $dV$ | area, volume | [[Double Integral]], [[Multiple Integration]] |
| $dS$, $d\mathbf{S}$ | surface area, oriented surface area | [[Surface Integral]], [[Flux]] |

**Choosing coordinates changes the element**, and the factor it changes by is the Jacobian:
$r\,dr\,d\theta$ in polar, $\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$ in spherical. See
[[Multiple Integration]].

The word also names the *equation* type: a [[Differential Equations|differential equation]] is one
relating differentials, which is the sense in which "separate the differentials and integrate both
sides" is a legitimate move rather than notation abuse.
